One of the biggest mistakes traders make is thinking the best entry has to be the earliest entry.

It doesn’t.

Sometimes the better trade comes after the stock has already proved you right.

$ARM this year is a perfect example. 🧵 https://t.co/eZ4Mnd33eJ

Early in the year, ARM was still messy.

The stock had spent months losing structure, failing rallies, and trading below the trend I actually wanted to see.

Could you try to catch the bottom there?

Sure.

But then you’re making a much harder bet: you’re trying to predict that the turn is happening before the market has really confirmed it.

That’s not what I’m looking for.

I don’t need the bottom. I need evidence that the trend has changed.

Then ARM started reclaiming structure.

Price moved back above the 21EMA, that average began flattening and eventually turning higher, and the stock started behaving differently.

That matters because a reclaim is only the first part of the process.

The next question is much more important:

Can the stock actually hold that reclaimed structure when sellers show up again?

That’s where the backtest comes in.

Look at what happened with ARM once that rising structure began holding.

The stock didn’t just bounce.

It started building on top of that structure, then progressively expanded higher as the trend strengthened.

That is the kind of trade I want.

Not because the entry is the cheapest possible.

But because the setup gives me a much clearer invalidation level, better context, and confirmation that the trend shift is real.

A slightly higher entry with much better information can be a far better trade.

Instead of chasing the initial move, I want to see price return to the now-rising structure and prove that former resistance is becoming support.

That gives me information I didn’t have at the lows.

The trend is improving.

The stock has already demonstrated demand.

And now I get to see whether buyers are willing to defend the area on weakness.

Reclaim → backtest → stabilization → re-acceleration.

That sequence is much more useful to me than trying to time the first reversal candle perfectly.

This is also why I don’t mind missing the first 10%, 15%, or sometimes even more of a move.

My goal isn’t to capture every dollar between the absolute low and the high.

My goal is to participate in the part of the move where the odds, structure, and risk/reward are working in my favor.

ARM eventually went from roughly the low-$100s into the $400s.

There was plenty of opportunity after the bottom was already obvious.

You don’t need to catch the turn. You need to know the turn is real.

Charts are easy to post.

The real value is understanding why the trade is there, what confirms it, where it’s wrong, and how to manage it from entry to exit.

USD/JPY at 154.2 and falling — yen at a 7-month high as shorts unwind into next week's near-certain BOJ hike. That's a tailwind for gold: the differential is now in the confirm zone (green in the subgraph label), and the 60-day gold/USDJPY correlation holds at −0.3, so the inverse premise is intact — the Yen differential signal (long gold) is valid.

But.  There's a catch.

/GC is off 0.67% at 4,446, back below its short MA — and the study reads "long-confirm N/A, gold not rising." 
So the macro backdrop is set up for a long, but price hasn't confirmed. Tailwind present, follow-through absent.

Regime check: my (validated) debasement detector (40-day gold/2Y correlation) is still reading normal/inverse at −0.36 as of last week.  That's not in the regime where the gold-long edge lives ... so, once again, the yen tailwind is a backdrop, not a green light.

What I and my algos are watching for: a green flip on /GC  — yen strength and gold turning up together.  That's the differential actually backing a long. Until then it's a supportive backdrop, not a signal.

Morning thoughts 9/8/26:

What if the best market indicator isn’t on your chart…it’s your last 10 trades?

If I’m 7/10 green on trades and my positions keep giving me cushion, I don’t care if the indices look ugly. The market is permitting me to gradually press.

If I’m 1/10 on trades while $SPY is ripping, I care even less about everyone screaming “risk-on” because MY feedback loop is telling me to get defensive. My aggressiveness should be dictated more by what my actual trades/setups are paying me than whatever market narrative sounds good that morning.

My P&L $$ obviously doesn’t predict the market, but it does tell me whether my edge is currently in sync with it...

...and knowing when to press vs. protect is 95% of the game.

These are my morning thoughts, enjoy!

If there are stocks you absolutely love right now but they are already completely extended, you need to do one of these two things:

1. Look elsewhere. It is the simplest, cleanest, and best possible answer. 
2. Buy a tiny fraction, but do not take a full position. This keeps you in the game but leaves you plenty of cash to scale in heavy on the dips. 

I promise you - chasing an entry that is already trading 15% to 20% away from its core EMA will never do you any good over the long haul. 

Every single day you will sit there staring at the screen, sweating and worried about that position, simply because you forced a high-risk, emotional entry. 

You either have the discipline to move on to the next setup, or you scale in with tiny sizes. Stop donating your liquidity to market makers.

My read on this:

1)  Skew Short Term 1.8329 against Medium 0.2767 and Long 0.2158. 
That's a front-end spike.  This happens to be a trigger candidate.  Given context, I interpret that as largely reflecting mechanical call overwriting flow.  In addition, I suspect a desk or two ... long the sector since July is buying puts to protect profit.  Seeing collaring, I believe that ST skew is arising from bullish holders, not bearish speculators.

2). Price is sitting on the call gamma flip. Close 64.07, call_gamma_flip 64.16 — a tenth of a percent below. Short-term call wall at 67.88 is 5.95% up; put wall 51.66 is 19.4% down. This is bullish in the near term.

3)  IV Term Structure 1.1011 — upward-sloping, and remember iv_1m 0.0724 is horizon-scaled: annualized that's 7.24% × √12 ≈ 25.1%, against XLE's realized vol of roughly 30% over the full history.  At roughly 25% annualized against ~30% realized, front-month IV is priced below XLE's historical volatility.  In other words, front-month IV is not obviously rich.

Conclusion
Nobody is positioned for downside, and the gamma structure is stabilizing.

Seasonality Is Context, Not a Signal

Seasonality is useful, but I think people misuse it when they treat it like a prediction engine. Just because September has historically been weak doesn’t mean you automatically short September.

What I care about is context.

What has this asset typically done during this period? How consistent has that tendency been? Is the current market actually confirming it?

Seasonality should help shape expectations. It shouldn’t replace price, trend, or risk management.

That’s how I use the Seasonality dashboard.

Looking at the dollar, more of the same with price trading below the lows of structure and below all key moving averages.

Precious metals in relation continue to consolidate its August move, with Gold in no mans land below the 10/20-EMA while Silver holds above its 20-EMA. Notably, Copper attempted a breakout of its 6 week holding pattern but faded somewhat by the close, perhaps more sideways is needed to build energy higher.

In cryptoland, the flag consolidations seen in the majors continue to be constructive - though eventual directional resolution remains to be seen.

Strong rotations out of one sector every few days while indices remain sideways make for a tough market environment - stay nimble.

Notes:

> Out with the software and in with selective hardware, the rotation trade remains in full force.

> This market remains in mindless chop which is expected, net high and net lows moving back and forth between positive - negative is not helping the cause.

> Markets for the most part has lacked momentum and it remains to be seen how long more it will stay this way (can be very long). That said, individual stock setups have worked - just trade what you see and be nimble.
